question: Data from the OECD and the World Resources Institute reveal the imminent risk of water scarcity all across Europe. Greece ranks 19th globally in terms of water scarcity risk, with 87 % of its territory facing an increased incidence of drought. Since 2019, the Greek Government has been addressing the issue of water scarcity with minimal effort, outdated announcements and very few projects.

It is worth noting that the situation is constantly deteriorating in areas of the country critical both for agricultural production and tourism. A prime example can be found in Thessaly, where rather than building flood defences, the government chooses to over-abstract from the limited water available in Lake Plastiras; a move with a direct impact on the area’s environment and future agricultural production.
In view of the above, the Commission is asked: 1.

Are provisions of the Water Framework Directive (2000/60/EC) on over-abstraction from surface water bodies, such as Lake Plastiras, being violated? Is the Commission aware of specific measures by the Greek Government to reverse the certain ecological disaster by means of projects for the protection and sustainable management of water (such as dams, reservoirs, groundwater recharge) and infrastructure?
What projects with a budget of over EUR 5 000 000 in the area of sustainable water management and replenishment are being financed through European funds?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (30.9.2025) Following a ruling of the Court of Justice of the EU1 whereby Greece was declared to have failed to fulfil its obligations under the Water Framework Directive2, the third River Basin Management Plans were finally adopted and submitted. The Commission is assessing them and intends to publish the results end of 2025.

Among the information provided, abstraction is a main reason for 6.1% of surface water bodies failing good ecological status. Lake Plastiras is identified as a highly modified waterbody with moderate ecological potential. According to the data reported by the Greek authorities, 14.1% of the groundwater bodies failed good quantitative status.

The Plan reported includes measures on infrastructure, dams, and water reuse. Once its assessment will be finalised, the Commission will, in line with the EU Water Resilience Strategy3, engage in a structured dialogue with all relevant Greek authorities to address the country-specific recommendations it will make.

Under the 2021–2027 Cohesion Policy4, public funding resources amounting to approximately EUR 626 million may support investments in sustainable water management in Greece. The Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) supports irrigation projects, with the Greek CAP Strategic Plan 2023-2027 providing up to EUR 260 million5.

However the selection and implementation of such projects are the responsibility of the Greek managing authorities. Therefore, the Commission does not have at its disposal a detailed list of individual projects.

The Commission also notes that proposed amendments to Regulations (EU) 2021/10586 and 2021/10567 highlight water resilience as a new EU priority, with flexibilities for Member States to increase support during the mid-term review of their programmes.
